of his own, in one volume for five guineas. From this
beginning he rose to considerable wealth, and he was wont
to remark, in after times, that his was "the first book
that ever made a Lord Mayor of London." He managed
his extensive commerce in prints throughout Europe with
so much judgment and liberality, that he had the opportu-
nity of employing the ablest artists of his time, and of
exporting largely, and in an advantageous manner, that
which had formerly been an article of import. Boydell's
property was greatly injured by the French Revolution, so
that his celebrated work, The Shakspeare Gallery, which he
had intended to bequeath to the public, was sold. He
served the office of Lord Mayor in 1791, and died in 1804.
Vivares is celebrated as being the first artist of any school
who was completely successful in rendering with fidelity
and spirit the landscapes of the great Italian masters. His
best works are from Claude. He learned his art rather late
in life, from Chatelain, but improved on the style of his
master, and became remarkable for the delicacy and light-
ness of his foliage, and for his broad, clear effect. He
acquired much greater freedom in etching than had been
before possessed, and bringing his plates to a state of con-
siderable finish with the point, he put on the last touches
with the graver.
The same mode of proceeding was pursued by Woollett,
whose landscapes are considered to present perfect models
of style. He has chiefly engraved from Wilson and
others; but he did not neglect historical subjects, as we
find by his "Death of General Wolfe" after West, and
some others. "In tracing the progress of this branch of
art," says a writer in the Edinburgh Encyclopædia, "we
cannot withhold our admiration from these two great
men, who, from the state of total insignificance and neglect
in which which they found it, raised it at once to such dignity
and perfection. The earliest landscapes we have of any
importance from the works of the great painters, are the
engravings of Bolswert, after the pictures of Rubens. They
are executed with his usual ability, but being entirely with
the graver, give a very inadequate idea of the character of
the foliage, the quality of surface of the several objects, or
the brilliancy and splendour of Rubens. The large set of
landscapes by Audran, after Nicolo Poussin, exhibits a
nearer approximation to the true style of landscape, being
executed with much greater delicacy, but from the un-
manageable nature of the graver with which they are
entirely executed, they are very defective in character and
spirit. The discrimination of Vivares and Woollett pointed
out the defects of their predecessors; and more particularly
in the works of the latter, we find all the truth of nature
united to all the beauties of mechanical skill."
John Browne was among the best landscape engravers of
this period. Several large works after Salvator Rosa, Both,
and other great masters, were executed by him in excellent
style. He likewise etched many plates, which were after-
wards finished by Woollett with the graver.
Artists in every department now rapidly multiplied in
England. Among these Sir Robert Strange holds a high
rank among engravers, and deserves especial notice. This
eminent artist was born 1721 at Pomona, one of the Orkney
Islands. After receiving a good education, he was invited
to the study of the law; that profession not suiting his
talents, and while yet uncertain what profession to choose,
he went on board a man-of-war; but he soon became dis-
gusted with a sea-life and returned home. In the mean
time his brother had accidentally discovered in his drawer
a variety of drawings and unfinished sketches, with which
he appears to have amused those hours that his friends
supposed were devoted to severer labours. These first
essays of genius being shown to Mr. Richard Cooper, a
gentleman who practised the fine arts at Edinburgh, they
were highly approved, and he at once proposed that young
Strange should be placed under his tuition. This was
accordingly done, and the pupil was making rapid progress,
when his studies were interrupted by the arrival of the
young Chevalier in Scotland. Strange, being urged by the
desire to gain the hand of Miss Isabella Lumisden, at her
request joined the rebel army, and continued to serve until
the total defeat of the Pretender's troops at Culloden. He lay
Edinburgh, and began to earn money by the sale of portraits
of the rival leaders in the rebellion, which he disposed of
privately at a guinea each. Having married the lady above
referred to, Strange proceeded to France to complete his
studies. At Rouen he gained the prize for design. At
Paris he studied engraving under the direction of the cele-
brated Le Bas. From this master he had the first hint of
the use of dry point, which he afterwards greatly improved,
and thus added superior beauties to his engravings.
In 1751 he settled in London, and devoted himself to
historical engraving. He soon established a high reputation
in this diffic difficult style of his art, of which he is considered
the father. In 1760 he visited Italy, where he was known
through the medium of his engravings, and was received
with honour and respect. He is the only Englishman
whose portrait is introduced in the painting in the Vatican
of the "Progress of Engraving."
The authority last quoted says of this artist, "He is
admirable for the breadth of his effect, and the beauty of
his execution; but his great excellency is the beauty and
softness of his female flesh. In this last, notwithstand-
ing the perfection that modern art has arrived at, in all
those great qualities that result from mechanical skill, he
has never been equalled by any master, as his engravings
from the works of Titian, Guido, Correggio, and the other
painters of the Italian schools, sufficiently show; but it is
deeply to be regretted that, with so many excellencies, his
drawing should be so incorrect, particularly in the extremi-
ties." He was appointed engraver to George the Third, and
received the honour of knighthood in 1787. He died on
the 5th July, 1792.
In landscape, besides Vivares, Woollett, and Browne,
many fine works from the old masters, by Byrne, Mason,
Wood, Elliott, Lowry, Wilson, Major, Earlom, and others,
show the the high standing of the English school; but in our
own times the extent to which works on almost every
subject are illustrated, is perhaps no real token for good to
the art. Artists are indeed multiplied, and there is an un-
exampled demand for the fruits of their industry; but the
study of the old masters is comparatively neglected, while
topography, antiquities, &c., usurp so large a share of study
and attention.
Among those who have illustrated the beautiful scenery
of this country, and shown that it is quite as capable of
pictorial effect as that of any foreign clime, we find one of
the first to be Paul Sandby, born at Nottingham, in 1732.
His early skill is evinced by the fact, that at the age of
sixteen he was employed as draughtsman under Mr. David
Watson, to complete a survey of the north and west
portions of the Highlands, for the late Duke of Cumber-
land. While thus occupied among romantic scenery, he
employed the leisure he could get from drawing plans, in
making sketches of the wild and picturesque spots he met
with. These he afterwards etched in small plates. Soon
afterwards he was introduced to the notice and patronage
of Sir Joseph Banks, and Sir Watkins William Wynne.
With the former he made a tour through North and South
Wales, and by y the latter he was employed to design the
most striking features of Welsh scenery. These views were
afterwards engraved in aquatinta. Sandby was one of the
original Members of the Royal Academy.
Of the engravers of the present day we purposely abstain
from giving an account. Perhaps their art was never more
highly prized, or more generally appreciated and encour-
aged. May this induce artists to take a high aim, and to
employ the improved facilities and advantages they enjoy,
in endeavouring to elevate and refine the public taste. It
is not often that we meet with men who unite the talents
of the painter and the engraver; yet it is much to be wished
that the number of such individuals should increase. The
advantage to an artist of being able to engrave his own
pictures is a most invaluable one. It is impossible that
another mind should grasp every idea intended to be con-
veyed by the artist, and grievous must be the disappoint-
ment in many cases, when in the engraving the painter
seeks in vain for the spirit which he intended to pervade
his work. The possibility of uniting the two arts, is mani-
fest in the case of Hogarth, and has also been proved in our
own time. May its desirability become more apparent, and
concealed in the Highlands during some months, and when | influence the practice of our men of talent!
